body_html:
Argentine slang is some of the most distinctive in the Spanish-speaking world. In Buenos Aires you will hear che to get someone’s attention, boludo between friends, laburo for work and quilombo for a mess. Much of it comes from lunfardo, the slang that grew in Buenos Aires in the late 1800s, partly from Italian immigrants. On top of that, Argentines use vos instead of tú, which changes the verbs. Here is what you need to understand Argentine conversations, and which words to handle with care.

Quick answer
  • Everyday: che, dale, bárbaro, copado, re (very)
  • Work and money: laburo, guita, mango
  • Careful: boludo is friendly among close friends, an insult otherwise.
  • Grammar: Argentines say vos sos, vos tenés, vos querés.
{{toc}}

Argentine slang for everyday conversations

WordMeaningExample
chehey (to get attention)Che, ¿venís mañana? (Hey, are you coming tomorrow?)
daleokay, sure, come on—¿Vamos? —¡Dale! (“Shall we go?” “Sure!”)
bárbarogreat, awesome¡Bárbaro, nos vemos! (Great, see you!)
copadocool, niceTu hermano es re copado. (Your brother is really cool.)
revery, reallyEstá re lindo el día. (It’s a really nice day.)
postafor real, really¿Posta? No te creo. (For real? I don’t believe you.)
qué bajónwhat a bummerSe suspendió el recital, qué bajón. (The concert was canceled, what a bummer.)
fiacalazinessHoy tengo fiaca. (I feel lazy today.)

Re is one of the most useful words to learn. Put it before almost any adjective to intensify it: re bueno, re caro, re cansado.

Work, money, people and things

WordMeaningExample
el laburo / laburarjob / to workTengo mucho laburo. (I have a lot of work.)
la guitamoneyNo tengo guita. (I have no money.)
un mangoa peso (money)No tengo un mango. (I’m broke.)
el pibe / la pibakid, young guy / girlLos pibes juegan al fútbol. (The kids are playing soccer.)
el quilombomess, chaos¡Qué quilombo el tráfico! (The traffic is chaos!)
morfarto eat¿Vamos a morfar algo? (Shall we grab something to eat?)
el bondithe busMe tomo el bondi. (I’ll take the bus.)
la birrabeer¿Unas birras? (A few beers?)
truchofakeEse reloj es trucho. (That watch is fake.)
chamuyarto sweet-talk, to BSNo me chamuyes. (Don’t sweet-talk me.)
{{image:2}}

Voseo: the grammar behind Argentine Spanish

You can’t understand Argentine slang without voseo. Instead of tú, Argentines use vos, with its own verb forms in the present tense and in commands:

Standard túArgentine vos
tú eresvos sos
tú tienesvos tenés
tú quieresvos querés
ven (come!)vení
mira (look!)mirá

The accent moves to the last syllable, which gives Argentine Spanish its rhythm. Combined with the sh sound for ll and y (yo sounds like “sho”), it is easy to recognize. For how this compares with other varieties, see {{link:latin-american-vs-spain-spanish|Latin American vs Spain Spanish}}, and for the formality side, {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}.

Boludo and other words to handle with care

Boludo (or boluda) is the most famous Argentine word, and the trickiest. Between close friends, it is affectionate and used constantly: ¿Qué hacés, boludo? (What’s up, dude?). Said with the wrong tone, or to someone you don’t know, it is an insult meaning “idiot”. Learners are safer recognizing it than using it.

  • mina: woman or girl. Common, but it can sound disrespectful.
  • forro: jerk, an insult.
  • concha: vulgar in Argentina, even though it means “shell” elsewhere.

Many of these words are recorded, with their country labels, in the Diccionario de americanismos from the Spanish language academies.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

A sample chat between friends

Sofi: Che, ¿qué hacés esta noche?
Hey, what are you doing tonight?

Nico: Nada, tengo re fiaca. Laburé todo el día.
Nothing, I feel so lazy. I worked all day.

Sofi: Dale, vení a casa. Pedimos algo para morfar y unas birras.
Come on, come over. We’ll order something to eat and a few beers.

Nico: ¡Bárbaro! Me tomo el bondi y voy.
Great! I’ll catch the bus and come over.

Notice hacés, laburé and vení: voseo appears in almost every sentence.

Mate, asado and cultural words

Some Argentine words are less slang than culture. El mate is the herbal drink shared from one cup, and refusing it politely is done by saying gracias, which means you are done. El asado is the barbecue, a social event in itself, and the person grilling is el asador. At an asado, it is common to applaud the cook: ¡Un aplauso para el asador!

For more on food and table talk, see {{link:family-dinner-spanish-phrases|Spanish phrases for family dinner}}.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

  • Calling a stranger boludo. It may start a fight.
  • Mixing tú and vos. Pick one. Argentines understand tú, but mixing sounds odd.
  • Using coger in Argentina. It is vulgar there. Use tomar for buses and taxis.
  • Thinking all of Argentina sounds like Buenos Aires. Córdoba and the north have their own accents and words.

Compare these with {{link:mexican-slang|Mexican slang}} and {{link:colombian-slang|Colombian slang}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Argentine slang makes much more sense once you hear voseo and lunfardo behind it. Start with che, dale, re and bárbaro, recognize boludo without rushing to use it, and enjoy one of the most musical varieties of Spanish. For other countries, see my guide to {{link:spanish-slang|Spanish slang}}.
